name: Backtracking
tagline: Choose, explore, un-choose. Cut dead branches early.
signals: pick numbers that sum to a target
find a word in a grid
template:
def subsets(A):
    out, path = [], []
    def go(i):
        if i == len(A):
            out.append(path[:])  # copy: path keeps changing
            return
        path.append(A[i])        # choose
        go(i + 1)                # explore
        path.pop()               # un-choose
        go(i + 1)                # explore without A[i]
    go(0)
    return out

print(subsets([1, 2]))  # -> [[1, 2], [1], [2], []]
complexity: O(2^N) or O(N!) worst case; pruning cuts the real work

blocks.html: Walking a maze: follow a corridor, and when it dead-ends, step back to the last fork and try the next way. Backtracking lists every option like this, and drops a whole branch as soon as it cannot lead to an answer.

blocks.text: Example: numbers that sum to a target

blocks.note: Build every subset, then grow one path and prune

blocks.html: Build the answer one choice at a time, and undo each choice after exploring it so the next branch starts clean. The speed comes from pruning: stop a branch the moment it cannot work.

options: path keeps changing; without a copy every saved answer ends up as the same list
blocks.why: path is one list you reuse. Appending it stores a reference, and the later pops empty it.

pitfalls: Save a copy (path[:]), not the list you keep changing.
Every append needs a matching pop on the way back.
Sort first, so you can break early and skip duplicates with if i > start and A[i] == A[i - 1]: continue.
